definition: Negligent means habitually careless; failing to take proper care.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word negligent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know negligent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A negligent pharmacist left the vaccine cooler unplugged through two summer weekends in a row.

Careless is milder than negligent — one forgotten email or one unchecked box is careless, a single slip shrugged off by lunchtime, while negligent names a habit of such slips in work someone was trusted to do.
Reckless goes further than negligent — the negligent driver never checks the mirrors, while the reckless one sees the ice and speeds up anyway.

Sloppy describes untidy execution — smeared ink, tangled cables, a report full of typos — whether or not anyone was owed better. Negligent needs a duty: someone was trusted to take proper care and, again and again, did not. A hobbyist can be sloppy; only the trusted party can be negligent.

Remiss is the polite, formal word for having let one duty slip — 'I was remiss in not replying.' It usually admits a single lapse, with mild regret. Negligent is heavier: a habitual failure to take proper care, the kind inspectors and courts get called about.

The server farm's negligent night technician had one job list: check the backup drives, rotate the tapes, note the temperatures.
What happened instead ran on from March to September — boxes ticked without a single tape rotated, alerts clicked away unread, spare drives never bought.
When the main drive died, there was nothing behind it.
Negligent is the exact word for that technician, because negligent means habitually careless, failing to take proper care — the duty was his, and the lapse ran on for half a year.
Careless is one dropped stitch; negligent is a pattern of them, in work someone was trusted to do.
Negligent is the odd one out in this unit: it names a failure of care, not a form of it.
Courts reach for it when a duty existed and nobody met it.
Keep it clear of lenient — a lenient judge chooses mildness on purpose, while a negligent one has stopped paying attention — and of docile, which is about being easily led, not failing anyone.

For three winters running, tenants at the Marbury flats reported the same broken boiler, and for three winters the landlord's office marked the tickets 'resolved' without sending anyone.
Radiators stayed cold; a pipe finally burst in February.
At the hearing, the tenants' lawyer laid out the pattern: forty-one maintenance requests, none answered, from an owner legally required to keep the building heated.
The landlord's counsel argued that the office had merely been disorganized.
The judge disagreed, and the word she chose mattered.
Disorganization is a mess; this was negligent — a duty of care, owed to people who paid rent for warmth, failed not once but habitually.
The fine was sized accordingly.
